notes: Detailed assessment on recoverability of inquest attendance costs in admitted clinical negligence proceedings; permission to appeal granted on point of principle.

enrichment.short_title: Recoverability of inquest costs in clinical negligence proceedings
key_facts: Clinical negligence proceedings under the Fatal Accidents Act proceeded on admitted liability, with costs limited to liability and causation.
The claimants attended and participated in the related inquest, incurring counsel costs for attendance and preparation.
The defence argued costs of one action cannot be costs of another and relied on Wright v Bennett and related authorities.
Correspondence showed the inquest involvement was motivated by facilitating the negligence claim and securing a neglect verdict.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Detailed assessment before a costs master on whether inquest-related costs were recoverable under the costs order.
enrichment.outcome: Inquest costs held recoverable as of and incidental to the clinical negligence proceedings where reasonably incurred; permission to appeal granted on the point of principle.
enrichment.ratio: Costs of an inquest may be of and incidental to other proceedings where the purpose for which the costs were incurred was that of the party incurring them, not the formal purpose of the inquest; the rule that costs of one action cannot be costs of another is not absolute and was distinguished on its facts from Wright, Department of Health v Envoy Farmers, Aiden Shipping and Contractreal.
legal_issues: Whether costs of attending and preparing for an inquest are recoverable in clinical negligence proceedings
Meaning of costs of and incidental to proceedings
Whether inquest participation beyond a noting brief was reasonable
Whether permission to appeal should be granted on a point troubling lower courts
linked_authorities: Wright v Bennett [1948] 1 KB 601
Department of Health v Envoy Farmers Limited [1976] 1 WLR 1018
Aiden Shipping Co Ltd v Interbulk Ltd [1985] 1 WLR 1222
Contractreal Ltd v Davies [2001] EWCA Civ 928
East Coast Aggregates v Para-Pagan (Clarke J, 8 August 1996, unreported)
Re Gibson (Settlement Trusts) [1981] Ch 179

notes: Dental negligence CFA success fee assessment; recoverability pre-issue, relief from sanctions, and 20% uplift are clearly resolved.

enrichment.short_title: CFA success fee recoverability after pre-action settlement
key_facts: A dental negligence claim settled for £25,000 plus costs before proceedings were issued under a CFA dated 10 January 2001.
The defendant was not notified of the funding arrangement until after costs-only proceedings began.
The claimant sought a 90% success fee; the defendant argued total irrecoverability and alternatively 20%.
The clinical disputes pre-action protocol applied but did not mandatorily require funding disclosure.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Preliminary issues at detailed assessment on recoverability of a success fee, relief from sanctions, and appropriate uplift percentage.
enrichment.outcome: Success fee held recoverable for the pre-issue period because CPR 44.3B(1)(c) did not bite before proceedings; relief from sanctions would have been refused; success fee limited to 20%.
enrichment.ratio: Under CPR 44.15 and CPD section 19.2(5), notice of funding is mandatory once proceedings start but only recommended pre-issue; PDP paragraph 4A.1 uses 'should' not 'must' and does not impose a compulsory pre-action obligation; where settlement precedes issue, failure to notify does not automatically bar recovery, though late relief applications and prejudice may matter once proceedings exist.
legal_issues: Whether failure to serve notice of funding bars recovery of a success fee
Whether PDP paragraph 4A.1 applies before issue of proceedings
Whether relief from sanctions under CPR 3.9 should be granted
What success fee percentage was reasonable for a dental negligence claim

notes: Withdrawn VAT delay challenge against Customs; hopeless claim costs order after interim relief refused.

enrichment.short_title: Deluni Mobile VAT repayment delay challenge costs
key_facts: Deluni Mobile, a repayment trader in mobile telephones, challenged unreasonable delay in HMRC decisions on VAT returns for September and October 2003.
Interim relief was refused by Pitchford J on 13 February 2004 and the permission application was withdrawn.
By the hearing HMRC had made decisions allowing appeals, but the company had ceased trading from 12 December 2003.
The claimant sought contribution to costs; HMRC had consented to withdrawal on each side paying own costs.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Costs hearing following withdrawal of judicial review permission application concerning VAT repayment delay.
enrichment.outcome: Claimant denied its costs; ordered to pay half of HMRC costs of the acknowledgment of service, assessed at £5,000 in broad terms.
enrichment.ratio: Proceedings seeking detailed disclosure of HMRC fraud investigations into carousel or missing-trader VAT chains were misconceived where no evidence showed enquiries were unreasonable or disproportionately delayed; HMRC were not obliged to explain investigation detail to taxpayers, though hopeless claims may attract costs even after sensible withdrawal.
legal_issues: Whether HMRC delay in processing VAT repayment claims was unlawful
Whether HMRC must disclose detailed investigation content
Appropriate costs order after withdrawal of a hopeless claim
Application of Mount Court costs principles
linked_authorities: Mount Court Limited (Auld LJ at paragraph 76)

confidence.notes: Merits and costs outcome are clear though permission was withdrawn before final refusal.

notes: Court of Appeal resolves Employment Rights Act 1996 section 218(5) continuity when partnership dissolves to sole principal.

enrichment.short_title: Employment continuity after solicitor partnership dissolution
key_facts: Hughes Hooker dissolved after partner Jack Bielecki was struck off on 6 March 2001; staff were dismissed effective 30 March 2001.
Mrs Stevens and Mr Marc claimed unfair dismissal against Bielecki and Michael Bower as continuing partners.
The EAT held partnership dissolved by operation of law but section 218(5) preserved continuity when Bower continued as sole principal.
Mr Bower appealed, relying on Harold Fielding Ltd v Mansi.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal on construction of section 218(5) ERA 1996 following Employment Tribunal and EAT decisions.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; employment continuity preserved until 30 March 2001; permission to appeal to the House of Lords refused.
enrichment.ratio: Section 218(5) ERA 1996 is intended to protect employees when partnership membership changes and applies where a two-partner firm becomes a sole proprietorship after dissolution; 'employment with the partners' includes employment with any one of them who was previously the employer as partner, displacing the narrower reading in Mansi.
legal_issues: Whether partnership dissolution on striking off dissolved the employer for employment purposes
Whether section 218(5) covers transition from partnership to sole principal
Whether section 218(2) also applied
Appropriate use of purposive construction for pre-EEC employment legislation
linked_authorities: Harold Fielding Ltd v Mansi [1974] ICR 347
Wynne v Hair Control [1978] ICR 870
Jeetle v Elster [1985] ICR 389
Allen & Son v Coventry [1980] ICR 9

confidence.notes: Ratio on section 218(5) is definitive. Section 218(2) was raised late and not finally determined.

notes: Long hackney carriage licence increase JR; wide discretion and TPI survey interpretation upheld with costs reductions.

enrichment.short_title: Reading hackney carriage licence increase judicial review
key_facts: Reading Borough Council resolved on 18 June 2003 to grant 30 additional hackney carriage licences, up from 138.
Transport Planning International recommended 8 new licences to meet significant unmet demand across the borough.
The committee chose option 3, issuing more than 8 licences without full de-restriction, citing town-wide demand and illegal private hire plying.
Reading Taxi Association challenged the decision as irrational and misreading the survey.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of a licensing committee decision to increase hackney carriage plates, with subsequent costs argument and summary assessment.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; council entitled to costs subject to reductions on solicitor time and telephone charges.
enrichment.ratio: Councils have a wide discretion to increase hackney carriage licences and need only restrict numbers where significant unmet demand is absent; choosing 30 licences over a survey minimum of 8 was not irrational where councillors relied on local knowledge, police support, expert officer advice, and evidence of wider unmet demand beyond Reading Station.
legal_issues: Lawfulness of increasing licences beyond TPI recommended minimum
Whether the survey was limited to Reading Station
Wednesbury irrationality of committee reasoning
Whether alternative sites or sequential policy applied
Discretionary costs where ADR was attempted pre-issue
linked_authorities: R v Great Yarmouth Borough Council, ex parte Sawyer (1989) RTR 297

confidence.notes: Merits decision and main costs order are clear. Detailed costs were summarily adjusted.

notes: Habeas corpus refused for bankrupt contemnor; committal challenge must go to Court of Appeal under Administration of Justice Act 1960.

enrichment.short_title: Habeas corpus refused for bankrupt contemnor
key_facts: Geoffrey Harold Scriven was adjudged bankrupt and failed to attend his public examination, later refusing to give evidence on 29 August 2001.
He was committed to six months imprisonment for contempt in absentia on 5 July 2002 and arrested under a warrant in March 2004.
Lilian Rayne applied for habeas corpus on his behalf; Scriven was a section 42 vexatious litigant.
Scriven argued invalid committal, defective forms, and that the August 2001 hearing was not a resumed public examination.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for leave to issue a writ of habeas corpus concerning detention at HM Prison Strangeways Manchester.
enrichment.outcome: Application refused; section 42 leave granted to appeal committal to the Court of Appeal if required; extension of time for committal appeal left to Court of Appeal.
enrichment.ratio: Habeas corpus is not the proper route to challenge a lawful committal sentence by a court of competent jurisdiction except in exceptional circumstances; defects in committal forms causing no prejudice do not render detention unlawful, and contempt findings should be challenged by appeal under section 13(2)(b) Administration of Justice Act 1960.
legal_issues: Whether habeas corpus lies to challenge a committal for contempt
Validity of committal and arrest warrant documentation
Whether the August 2001 hearing was a public examination
Effect of section 42 vexatious litigant order on appeals
linked_authorities: Linnett v Coles [1987] 1 QB 555
Nicholls v Nicholls [1997] 1 WLR 314
ex parte Waldron [1986] 1 QB 824

confidence.notes: Procedural route and refusal are clear. Factual disputes about service and hearing purpose were noted but not finally resolved on merits.

notes: Seven-ground JR over Bicester asylum accommodation centre; Crown immunity and Circular 18/84 procedure upheld.

enrichment.short_title: Bicester asylum accommodation centre planning challenge
key_facts: The Home Office proposed a 750-person asylum accommodation centre at former DSDC land in Bicester via a Notice of Proposed Development.
An inspector recommended refusal after a 14-day inquiry; the First Secretary of State approved the development on 18 August 2003.
Development was to be design-build-operate by a contractor granted a lease before works commenced.
Cherwell District Council challenged procedure, alternative sites, sequential policy, local services impact, and rural location.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of approval of Crown development under Circular 18/84 non-statutory procedure.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed on all seven grounds; permission to appeal refused with 21-day extension to apply to Court of Appeal.
enrichment.ratio: Development by a DBO contractor on Crown land for Home Office asylum policy purposes is development by or on behalf of the Crown immune from ordinary planning control; section 299 does not compel use of the statutory procedure, and refusal to follow the inspector on planning merits was lawful where alternative sites, sequential tests, and service impacts were reasonably addressed.
legal_issues: Whether Crown development required Part XIII section 299 procedure
Whether DBO lease-before-build development retained Crown immunity
Relevance of alternative sites and sequential approach
Impact on local services and rural location justification
Whether temporary permission should have been considered

notes: TCC cross-appeals on Party Wall Act damage at Sandbanks; underpinning, rent loss and diminution in value awarded.

enrichment.short_title: Party Wall Act damage from Sandbanks excavation
key_facts: Bemstone Homes excavated and piled a deep site at 6 Salter Road Sandbanks to build two four-storey houses adjacent to Dr and Mrs Young's property at number 8.
Party wall notices were served late; piling caused severe vibration, cracking, and tenants vacated the property.
The developer's own correspondence criticised sloppy piling workmanship adjacent to number 8.
Expert evidence established no significant pre-existing structural damage before January 2001 works.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Cross-appeals in the Technology and Construction Court on party wall awards for damage, remedial works, and compensation.
enrichment.outcome: Claimants succeeded; underpinning and remedial works of about £126,312 ordered; loss of rent, diminution in value, and party wall costs recoverable under section 7(2).
enrichment.ratio: Where adjoining excavation and piling works on sand without timely party wall compliance cause structural damage, the building owner must compensate for loss and damage under the Party Wall Act; causation may be inferred from timing, tenant evidence, and the developer's own concerns about defective piling and inadequate lateral restraint.
legal_issues: Whether damage to number 8 was caused by works at number 6
Pre-existing condition and schedule of condition evidence
Whether underpinning was necessary
Recoverability of loss of rent and diminution in value
Quantum of site and property value

confidence.notes: Findings on causation, remedy, and heads of loss are detailed. Some disclosure concerns about developer records were noted.

notes: CA criticises deciding share transfer notice construction at pre-action disclosure stage; limited disclosure ordered.

enrichment.short_title: Pre-action disclosure and Lynx Articles construction
key_facts: Philip Rose sought CPR 31.16 pre-action disclosure from Lynx Express and Bridgepoint Capital concerning transfers of beneficial interests in shares.
Lynx's 1997 Articles contained elaborate pre-emption and Investor consent provisions, with Article 2.6 deeming equitable dispositions to be share transfers.
Bridgepoint held shares as nominee for limited partnerships without giving Transfer Notices on beneficial interest transfers.
The deputy judge decided the notice construction issue against Mr Rose and dismissed the application.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Permission to appeal and appeal against refusal of pre-action disclosure under CPR 31.16.
enrichment.outcome: Permission granted; appeal allowed; limited pre-action disclosure ordered of transfer documents and exemption-supporting material.
enrichment.ratio: Courts should hesitate to determine core substantive construction issues on pre-action disclosure applications; it is normally enough that the anticipated claim is properly arguable with real prospect of success, and Article 11 transfer notice obligations alongside Article 2.6 deeming provisions raise sufficiently arguable issues to justify limited disclosure without finally resolving construction.
legal_issues: Conditions for pre-action disclosure under CPR 31.16(3)
Whether Articles require Transfer Notices on beneficial interest dispositions by non-members
Interaction of Articles 2.6, 10, 11 and 13
Propriety of preliminary determination of construction at pre-action stage

notes: Complex s106 highway contribution dispute; planning obligation not discharged by breach but damages inquiry ordered for delay.

key_facts: Trustees of a Neasden temple site paid £550,000 under a 1992 section 106 agreement for junction improvements linked to Fairclough's residential development permission.
The council delayed for years pursuing a left-hand slip road before implementing traffic signalisation and footway works completed by 2003.
The Mission demanded repayment from August 1999; most of the contribution was spent on signalisation including Braemar Avenue junction.
Clause 5 required the Engineer to certify works necessary due to increased highway use from the development.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Chancery claim for repayment of a section 106 highway contribution and damages for delayed works.
enrichment.outcome: Repayment claim failed because a planning obligation cannot be discharged by repudiatory breach; Engineer's opinion upheld; damages inquiry ordered for failure to complete works by end of 1996.
enrichment.ratio: A section 106 planning obligation to permit draw-down of deposited sums is a statutory planning obligation modifiable only under section 106A, not by acceptance of repudiatory breach; the Engineer's opinion on necessity must be honest and supported by evidence, while an implied term requires reasonable endeavours to complete works within a reasonable time after the certificate date.
legal_issues: Whether repudiatory breach discharges a section 106 agreement
Construction of 'necessary' highway improvements in clause 5
Whether the Engineer acted reasonably in certifying signalisation works
Whether Braemar Avenue signalisation fell within the junction works
Damages for delayed completion after October 1994
